caseNote: 실제 기업 (DaimlerChrysler 합병) + 실제 연구 (Hall, Meyer) + 가상 적용 (사내 글로벌 팀, 리모델링 회사)
insight: 문화 차이는 음식이나 언어가 아니라 같은 말과 행동이 어떤 뜻으로 읽히는가의 차이다. 그래서 말을 번역하는 것만으로는 부족하고, 그 뜻을 확인해야 한다.
misconception: 문화 차이는 언어, 음식, 명절 같은 겉모습의 문제라서 번역과 예절만 챙기면 해결된다.

sources.text: Hall, E. T. (1976). Beyond Culture. Anchor Books. (high-context / low-context communication)
Meyer, E. (2014). The Culture Map. PublicAffairs. (eight scales, including communicating, evaluating, deciding and trusting)
Daimler AG press release on the sale of a majority stake in Chrysler to Cerberus Capital Management (May 2007)
Contemporary business press coverage of the 1998 Daimler-Benz and Chrysler merger

factChecks.note: Daimler-Benz와 Chrysler의 합병은 1998년이며 '대등한 합병(merger of equals)'으로 발표되었습니다. 2007년 Daimler가 Chrysler 지분 약 80%를 Cerberus에 매각했습니다. 카드에는 금액 없이 'sold most of Chrysler'로만 적었습니다. 게시 전 보도자료로 재확인하세요.
합병 후 의사결정 방식, 회의의 격식, 임원 보수 차이를 둘러싼 마찰은 당시 언론과 경영 사례 연구에서 널리 다뤄졌습니다. 다만 실패 원인을 문화 하나로 단정하지 않도록 7번 카드에서 다른 원인도 언급했습니다.

Meyer의 The Culture Map은 8개 척도(communicating, evaluating, persuading, leading, deciding, trusting, disagreeing, scheduling)를 제시합니다. 카드에는 그중 4개만 일반적인 표현으로 소개했습니다. '문화는 상대적 위치로 봐야 한다'는 주장도 Meyer의 핵심 논지입니다.
2번, 8번 카드의 사내 팀과 리모델링 회사는 설명용 가상 사례입니다. 특정 국가를 지목하지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Why "Very interesting" might mean no
body: In 1998, Germany's Daimler-Benz and America's Chrysler joined forces. It was announced as a merger of equals between two proud carmakers.
Less than ten years later, Daimler sold most of Chrysler. There were many reasons. One kept coming up in the accounts: the two sides often heard the same words and understood different things.

image.label: Two teams at one table, speech bubbles that don't match
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 긴 회의 테이블 양쪽에 두 팀이 앉아 있고, 한쪽이 말한 말풍선이 건너편에 도착하면서 모양과 색이 바뀌는 연출. 자동차 회사 로고, 국기, 실제 브랜드는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: No one objected. Is that a yes?
body: You lead a product team in a large company. You present a new plan to colleagues in an office abroad. They nod, say "Very interesting, we will study it," and raise no objections.
Two weeks later, nothing has moved. What do you do?

options.text: Go ahead. Silence in the meeting meant agreement
options.feedback: You save time now, but you may be building on a plan they quietly rejected. The delay is often the real answer.

options.text: Ask a trusted colleague there, one-on-one, what concerns people have
options.feedback: It costs a call, but private conversations are often where disagreement is safe to voice. You learn what the meeting didn't say.

options.text: Email everyone asking for objections by Friday
options.feedback: Clear and fair by your own rules. But if open disagreement feels rude to them, a group email gets you more polite silence.

cards.title: Same company, different rules.
body: Accounts from the time describe friction over how decisions were made, how formal meetings should be, and even how executives were paid.

Neither side was wrong. Each followed rules it had never needed to say out loud. When those rules met, a careful plan could look like stalling to one side, and a quick decision could look reckless to the other.
The org chart said one company. Day to day, it often worked like two.

cards.title: Cultural differences
body: **Cultural differences** are the unwritten rules a group shares about how to speak, decide, disagree and build trust.

They matter in business because the same behavior sends different signals. Silence can mean agreement or refusal. A blunt comment can be honest or insulting. A long meeting can be careful work or a waste of time.
Translating the words is the easy part. Reading what they mean is the hard part.

image.label: One gesture, two meanings
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 가운데 고개를 끄덕이는 사람 하나, 양쪽으로 화살표가 갈라져 왼쪽은 "I agree", 오른쪽은 "I hear you" 라벨. 단순하고 밝은 색, 국기나 민족 고정관념 표현은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Where the hidden rules show up.
body: Anthropologist Edward T. Hall described **high-context** cultures, where much of the meaning sits in tone and relationship, and low-context ones, where meaning sits in the explicit words.
Writer Erin Meyer later mapped business cultures on eight scales. Four are especially useful:
list: **Communicating:** said outright, or read between the lines
**Giving feedback:** direct criticism, or softened and private
**Deciding:** the boss decides, or the group agrees first
**Trusting:** built by doing good work, or by building a relationship first

cards.title: You're only direct compared to someone.
body: Meyer's key point is that culture is about relative position. A manager can seem blunt to one colleague and vague to another, without changing a word.
This applies inside one country too. A head office and a regional team, or a sales team and an engineering team, can each have their own rules.
So the useful question is not "What is their culture?" It's "Where are they compared with us, on this issue?"

image.label: A sliding scale with three people placed on it
image.brief: 가로 눈금자 하나에 "Direct"와 "Indirect" 양 끝. 가운데 사람 한 명이 서 있고, 왼쪽 사람에게는 '돌려 말하는 사람', 오른쪽 사람에게는 '직설적인 사람'으로 보이는 말풍선. 국가 이름이나 국기는 표기하지 않음.

cards.title: Patterns are a first guess, not a verdict.
body: Cultural patterns describe groups on average. The person in front of you may not fit. Treat them as stereotypes and you insult people who never asked to be a type.
Culture also gets blamed for problems that have other causes. DaimlerChrysler faced tough car markets and costly strategy choices too.
Use patterns to form a question, then check it with the actual people.

cards.title: Now it's a renovation company.
body: Your kitchen renovation firm expands to a new country. At home, you send a clear written quote and start within a week. Here, customers praise your quotes but keep delaying.
A local employee says people expect to meet the owner, talk for a while and get to know them before signing. What do you change?

options.text: Cut prices 10% to make the quote harder to refuse
options.feedback: You give away margin to fix a problem that isn't about price. Customers may still wait, now at a lower price.

options.text: Add an owner visit before the quote, and keep the clear written terms
options.feedback: It costs time per job, but it builds the trust customers need first. You keep the clarity that makes your firm reliable.

options.text: Keep your process. Customers will adapt to efficiency
options.feedback: You protect your routine, but you ask every customer to change their rules for you. Local rivals who meet them first win the job.

cards.softwareNote: The same split shows up in software sales. In some markets a free trial and a self-serve checkout are enough. In others, buyers expect a call and a relationship with a real person before they sign.

cards.title: Check what people mean, not just what they say.
body: Cultural differences live in how people agree, disagree, decide and trust. The words can be perfectly translated and still be misread.
**Try it today:** think of a colleague or customer from a different background. Ask them one question: "When someone here says yes, how do you know they really mean it?"
